title: Harbour & Pine Sets Up Its Campaign Project
description: A homeware retailer's marketing team moves from separate chats to one shared Claude Project for a spring campaign that includes 120 in-store signs. They brief Claude for a data-to-copy task, set up the Project, choose between uploads and a live connector, trace a stale price, fit legal review to a print deadline, and keep customer identities out of a segment analysis.

scenario.background: Harbour & Pine's spring campaign launches in three weeks across email, social and 120 in-store signs, and every price and offer it states has to be right. The company is a homeware retailer with 12 shops, and its six-person marketing team uses Claude on a Team plan. Until now everyone has worked in their own chats, so some writers paste the brand guide every time, others don't, and copy quality varies from one campaign to the next. Maya, the marketing lead, wants one shared Project so every draft starts from the same voice, product facts and rules. Prices come from a product sheet that changes several times a week, and the CRM team holds the loyalty data the campaign will target.

characters.name: Maya Okafor
characters.concern: She wants the campaign to launch on time, with every writer working from the same shared setup.

characters.name: Leo Brandt
characters.concern: He writes most of the copy, including the 120 sign texts, and is tired of Claude's generic first drafts.

characters.name: Sana Iqbal
characters.concern: She wants to target the campaign at loyalty members whose past purchases fit the spring range.

characters.name: Tom Reyes
characters.concern: He signs off prices and offers, can review about 40 items before Friday's print deadline, and guards customer data.

questions.stem: Leo has the product team's export with four columns: SKU, product name, old price and new price. He needs 120 sign texts of up to 60 characters each. Which request will give him signs he can check and print?
options: Paste the export and ask Claude to write short, punchy sign copy for each product in the spring range, ready to print
Name the columns, show one finished sign, give the 60-character limit and £0.00 format, and say to write 'price missing' rather than guess
Ask Claude for ten creative headline styles first, agree the strongest one with Maya, then paste the export and ask for the 120 signs in that style
Upload last year's spring signs with the export and ask Claude to work out the layout and price style from those examples
questions.explanation: A technical brief needs the columns, an example and the rules. B is correct: Claude works only from what's on the page, so naming the columns, showing one finished sign, and stating the limit, the price format and what to write when a price is missing gives signs Leo can check line by line. A is wrong because Claude fills every gap with a default. C is wrong because headline style isn't the gap. D is wrong because old signs may carry last year's rules.

questions.stem: Maya creates the shared "Spring campaign" Project for the six-person team. Which setup gives each chat the same starting point without letting anyone quietly change the rules?
options: Instructions: the 40-page brand guide pasted in full. Knowledge: product fact sheets. Sharing: Maya and Leo "Can edit", the others "Can view"

Instructions: voice, audience, format and "flag any price not in the current sheet". Knowledge: brand guide, fact sheets, approved examples. Sharing: "Can edit" for the whole team so anyone can fix errors
Instructions: each writer's own style preferences. Knowledge: brand guide, fact sheets, examples. Sharing: Maya and Leo "Can edit", others "Can view"
Instructions: voice, audience, format and "flag any price not in the current sheet". Knowledge: brand guide, fact sheets, approved examples. Sharing: Maya and Leo "Can edit", others "Can view"
questions.explanation: Rules go in instructions, reference files in knowledge. D is correct: instructions set how Claude behaves in each chat, knowledge holds the documents every chat draws on, and "Can view" lets the rest of the team use the Project without changing it. A is wrong because a 40-page guide belongs in knowledge, not instructions. B is wrong because "Can edit" for everyone lets anyone change the shared rules. C is wrong because personal preferences belong in each writer's account instructions.

questions.stem: The current prices live in a Google Sheet that the product team updates several times a week. Leo wants to add it from Drive to the shared Project's knowledge so it stays in sync. What should Maya tell him?
options: Adding Drive files to knowledge works in private Projects, not shared ones, so writers read the live sheet via the Drive connector in the chat
Add the sheet from Drive to the Project's knowledge anyway, because a Google file added from Drive keeps syncing to its latest version for everyone
Download the sheet each Monday and upload the new copy to knowledge, so the Project holds this week's prices for the whole team
Paste the current prices into the Project instructions, and ask whoever changes a price in the sheet to update them there too
questions.explanation: Upload what rarely changes; connect what keeps changing. A is correct: adding Drive files to Project knowledge works in private Projects and is disabled in shared ones, so in this shared Project each writer uses the Drive connector in the chat, and Claude sees only what that writer's account can open. The brand guide and fact sheets stay uploaded. B is wrong because the option isn't available here. C is wrong because a Monday upload is stale by Wednesday. D is wrong because instructions hold rules, not changing data.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, three shop signs show last month's price for the oak garden bench, although the live sheet is correct. Leo's chats use the Drive connector, as agreed. How should Maya find and fix the cause?
options: Switch the Project's chats to a more capable model so Claude reads the live sheet more carefully, then reprint the three signs in the affected shops
Add "use the newest prices you can find" to the Project instructions, then ask Leo to regenerate the bench signs
Ask Claude which file the bench price came from, remove any old copy it names, add a dated note to the instructions and retest the sign
Ask Tom to check the price on each sign from now on, since the Project setup has shown it can't be trusted with prices
questions.explanation: Diagnose before you fix: one source per fact. C is correct: asking Claude which file it used is quick evidence for a source problem. Here it names a copy of the sheet Leo uploaded in week one "as a backup", a second, stale source. Removing it, recording the change, retesting the same sign and telling the team fixes the cause. A is wrong because a bigger model repeats a stale figure fluently. B is wrong because the old file stays readable. D is wrong because it treats the symptom.

questions.stem: The signs print on Friday. Maya says the shops have booked the launch; Tom can properly review about 40 items by then and would rather delay. 30 signs state a price or offer, and 90 only describe products. What is the best plan?
options: Delay the launch until Tom has reviewed each of the 120 signs, since a wrong shelf price creates a legal problem for the shops
Print on Friday and have Tom review a random sample of 40 of the 120 signs, spreading his time evenly across the batch
Print on Friday without legal review, since the signs came from the Project's approved rules and the live price sheet
Tom fully reviews the 30 price and offer signs, authors check the 90 description signs, and Tom samples some of those
questions.explanation: Scale review to what each item states. D is correct: the deciding fact is that only 30 signs carry prices or offers, which fits Tom's capacity of about 40, so the risky category gets full review and the descriptions get an author check plus a sample, and Maya keeps her date. A is wrong because it holds up low-risk copy. B is wrong because a random sample can miss wrong prices. C is wrong because following Project rules isn't review, and the bench showed a stale price can slip through.

questions.stem: Sana wants to upload the full loyalty export (names, emails, postcodes, purchase history, loyalty IDs) so Claude can find spring segments and then produce the list of customers to email. Tom points to the data policy. What should she do?
options: Drop names and emails, swap loyalty IDs for a made-up key, keep region, category and month; Claude finds segments, Sana builds the list in the CRM
Upload the full export in the company's Team workspace, since that workspace is approved and the analysis stays in-house
Upload the full export, have Claude produce the segments and the email list, then ask it not to keep the customer details
Upload the export to her personal Pro account with memory turned off, so the customer details stay out of the team's shared workspace and chat history
questions.explanation: Keep identities out of analysis that doesn't need them. A is correct: finding segments needs region, category and month, not who the customers are, so Sana removes names and emails, replaces loyalty IDs with a made-up key, and applies the chosen segments in the CRM herself. The customer list never goes into Claude. B is wrong because an approved workspace doesn't make unneeded identities necessary. C is wrong because data is shared once uploaded. D is wrong because a personal account sits outside approved tools.

keyLearnings: A technical brief needs the columns, an example and the rules, including what to write when a value is missing.
Shared Projects take live files through connectors, not knowledge, while stable reference files stay uploaded.
Keep one source per fact: a stale backup copy is a second source, so trace an answer to its file before changing anything.
Scale review to what each item states, and keep identities out of analysis that doesn't need them.
